stride.title: Counterfeit dependencies can impersonate the public package registry to the build runner
stride.description: An attacker able to substitute a response on the internet-facing dependency path can impersonate `entity:public-package-registry` to `process:build-runner` over `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`. The runner explicitly does not verify package signatures, so it accepts a counterfeit package as the named registry dependency. Second-order: the runner incorporates that code into an image, which can be pushed to `store:image-registry`, selected through `process:deploy-controller`, and pulled by the fleet represented by `process:store-server`.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low because exploitation requires an attacker to substitute dependency content on the crossing from `boundary:build-environment` to `boundary:internet`, although package-signature authentication is stated absent. Impact is high because code accepted by `process:build-runner` can be propagated through `store:image-registry` and `process:deploy-controller` to approximately 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, which are tagged `availability-critical` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Verify signed dependency provenance before building
mitigations.detail: Require `process:build-runner` to verify signatures and trusted publisher identity for every package obtained through `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, rejecting unsigned or untrusted artifacts.

mitigations.summary: Make transport authentication explicit for registry resolution
mitigations.detail: Use TLS with full certificate-chain validation and document `encryption_in_transit` and endpoint verification for the public-registry flow, reducing opportunities to substitute registry responses.

stride.title: A shared build token can be used to impersonate the build runner to the deploy controller
stride.description: An attacker who obtains the shared build token can present it on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` and act as `process:build-runner` to `process:deploy-controller`. Because the token is the same for every pipeline and has never been rotated, it does not provide a distinct, revocable workload identity. Second-order: the impersonator can select the image sha the estate should run, causing `process:store-server` instances to poll the controller and deploy the selected release across the store fleet.

grounds.text:
The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token
that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline
was set up.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the credential is shared by every pipeline, is long-lived without rotation, and crosses from `boundary:build-environment` to `boundary:corporate-network`; an attacker must obtain the token but does not need to defeat a per-workload identity. Impact is high because `process:deploy-controller` controls the release selected by approximately 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, which are tagged `availability-critical` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared token with per-workload short-lived identity
mitigations.detail: Authenticate `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` using a unique workload identity such as mTLS or short-lived audience-bound tokens, so each pipeline is independently attributable and revocable.

mitigations.summary: Rotate and scope the existing deployment credential
mitigations.detail: Until workload identity is deployed, rotate the shared token, store it in an appropriate secret-management mechanism, and restrict it to only the release-selection operation required by `process:build-runner`.

stride.title: A counterfeit image registry could be accepted by store servers if registry authentication is absent
stride.description: `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` crosses from `boundary:store-estate` to `boundary:build-environment`, but both its `authentication` and `encryption_in_transit` attributes are unknown. If those unknowns resolve to no verified registry server identity and certificate validation, an attacker with a position on the retail WAN could impersonate `store:image-registry` to `process:store-server` and provide a counterfeit image for the requested release. Second-order: each affected store server restarts the container it pulls, so one successful registry impersonation can affect the fleet represented by `process:store-server`. This draft is conditional on the undocumented authentication and transport controls; it does not assert that they are absent.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the store-to-registry flow crosses the retail WAN but exploitation requires an attacker to obtain an on-path or endpoint-substitution position; the relevant authentication and transit-encryption controls are undocumented. Impact is high because a counterfeit image would be restarted by the approximately 1,200 servers represented by `process:store-server`, which is tagged `availability-critical` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Require authenticated TLS for image pulls
mitigations.detail: Set explicit transport protection for `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`: use TLS 1.2+ with full certificate-chain validation and constrain registry certificate issuance through a private CA or workload identity.

mitigations.summary: Verify image provenance before restart
mitigations.detail: Require `process:store-server` to verify signed image provenance and an expected immutable digest before accepting content from `store:image-registry`, so a substituted registry endpoint cannot supply a trusted-looking image.

stride.title: Unsigned public dependency can be planted into released till images
stride.description: An attacker able to publish a substituted dependency at `entity:public-package-registry` can plant it through `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, because the build runner does not verify package signatures. `process:build-runner` incorporates the dependency into the container image it produces. Second-order, the image is published to `store:image-registry`, selected as a release, and pulled and restarted by the store-server fleet, turning a package substitution into altered till-software behavior.

grounds.text: the lockfile is taken as given — the runner does not verify signatures on what it downloads

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies` crosses into `boundary:internet` and package-signature verification is stated absent, but the attacker must control or successfully substitute a package artifact. Impact is high: `process:build-runner` produces release images, and altered till software can reach the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Verify signed, immutable dependency artifacts
mitigations.detail: Require `process:build-runner` to verify package signatures against trusted publisher keys and enforce lockfile hashes before accepting packages from `entity:public-package-registry`.

mitigations.summary: Protect dependency retrieval in transit
mitigations.detail: Use authenticated TLS with certificate validation on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, while retaining signature verification as an end-to-end integrity control.

stride.title: Source can be modified in transit before the build runner compiles it
stride.description: If `encryption_in_transit: unknown` on `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source` means the cross-zone connection lacks authenticated integrity protection, an attacker positioned between the build environment and corporate network can alter the fetched source before `process:build-runner` compiles it. Second-order, the runner packages the altered code into an image in `store:image-registry`; once selected as the current release, store servers can deploy the altered till software. This is conditional on the currently unverified transport protection.

grounds.text: The build runner picks the merge up, fetches the source, resolves the dependency lockfile and produces a container image.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unverified `encryption_in_transit` attribute: the flow crosses from `boundary:build-environment` to `boundary:corporate-network`, but an attacker still needs an on-path position. Impact is high because a modified source build becomes a release image that can alter till software across the store estate.

mitigations.summary: Use mutually authenticated, integrity-protected Git transport
mitigations.detail: Set `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source` to authenticated TLS or SSH with host-key validation and require the runner to reject integrity failures.

mitigations.summary: Verify the commit before building
mitigations.detail: Require `process:build-runner` to verify approved signed commits and the expected commit object before producing an image, so a transport rewrite cannot become build input.

stride.title: Current-release selection can be rewritten on the runner-to-controller path
stride.description: If `encryption_in_transit: unknown` on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` resolves to no authenticated transport integrity, an attacker on the build-environment-to-corporate-network path can alter the image SHA sent to `process:deploy-controller`. The controller can then record an unintended existing image as the current release. Second-order, every `process:store-server` polls that record and may pull and restart on the attacker-selected release. This is conditional on the unverified transport protection, not an assertion that the connection is plaintext.

grounds.text: When the image is pushed the runner calls the deploy controller and asks it to make that image the current release.
Every store server asks the deploy controller once a minute what the current release is, and if it differs from what it is running it pulls that image from the registry and restarts the container.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown transport protection: the flow is a boundary crossing, although an attacker needs an on-path position between `boundary:build-environment` and `boundary:corporate-network`. Impact is high because `process:deploy-controller` selects the release consumed by the approximately 1,200-store fleet, whose servers are tagged `business-critical-data` and `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Mutually authenticate and integrity-protect release-selection calls
mitigations.detail: Use mTLS or equivalent authenticated encryption for `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` and bind the shared build token to a short-lived workload identity.

mitigations.summary: Require signed release manifests at the controller
mitigations.detail: Have `process:deploy-controller` accept only a build-signed release manifest that binds the approved image digest to the release change, rather than trusting an alterable SHA request.

stride.title: Release-poll responses can direct store servers to an altered release
stride.description: If the unknown encryption and authentication controls on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release` do not provide authenticated message integrity, an attacker on the retail-WAN path can alter the current-release SHA returned to `process:store-server`. The server treats that response as its release decision and then pulls the indicated image and restarts its till container. Second-order, an attacker able to affect this path broadly can cause altered or rollback releases across the store estate. This threat is conditional on the unverified flow controls.

grounds.text: Every store server asks the deploy controller once a minute what the current release is, and if it differs from what it is running it pulls that image from the registry and restarts the container.
Traffic between the stores and the corporate network goes over the retail WAN.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown authentication and encryption attributes: the retail-WAN flow crosses from `boundary:store-estate` to `boundary:corporate-network`, but exploitation requires a position on that path. Impact is high because `process:store-server` represents roughly 1,200 servers and is tagged `availability-critical` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate and encrypt release polling
mitigations.detail: Use mTLS with authenticated encryption on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release` and require each store server to validate the controller identity.

mitigations.summary: Verify a signed release manifest before restart
mitigations.detail: Make `process:store-server` verify a release manifest signed by the deployment authority and reject unrecognized, stale, or improperly authorized image references.

stride.title: Container image bytes can be modified while stores pull them over the WAN
stride.description: If `encryption_in_transit: unknown` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` means image retrieval lacks authenticated integrity protection, an attacker positioned on the retail-WAN path can alter container bytes delivered from `store:image-registry` to `process:store-server`. The receiving server then restarts the supplied image as till software. Second-order, compromising this shared retrieval path can propagate altered runtime behavior to many store servers. This is conditional on the unverified transport protection.

grounds.text: The image registry is reachable from the store estate over the WAN.
if it differs from what it is running it pulls that image from the registry and restarts the container.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown `encryption_in_transit` value: the image-pull flow crosses from `boundary:store-estate` to `boundary:build-environment`, while an attacker needs a WAN on-path position. Impact is high because the altered artifact executes as till software on `process:store-server`, which represents the 1,200-server estate and is tagged `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Use authenticated encryption for registry pulls
mitigations.detail: Require TLS with registry identity validation on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` so an on-path actor cannot substitute image bytes.

mitigations.summary: Enforce image-digest and signature verification
mitigations.detail: Configure `process:store-server` to pull immutable digests and verify trusted image signatures before restart, rejecting content that does not match the approved release manifest.

stride.title: Shared build token leaves release changes unattributable to a specific pipeline
stride.description: A holder of the shared credential can set a new current release through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` at `process:deploy-controller` and later deny having done so. The flow's token is stated to be the same for every pipeline, so a record naming that token or the build runner can narrow a disputed release change only to the population of pipeline holders, not establish which pipeline or actor selected the image SHA. A disputed change to the deployment record then propagates when `process:store-server` polls the controller and pulls the selected image across the estate; accountability for a release affecting approximately 1,200 stores collapses even if the controller retains an event record.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: exploiting the gap requires access to a pipeline that can present the shared token, but `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` crosses from `boundary:build-environment` into `boundary:corporate-network` and the shared credential cannot distinguish its holders. Impact is high: `process:deploy-controller` holds `business-critical-data`, and its release choice is consumed by `process:store-server` across the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Use a distinct, attributable deployment identity per pipeline
mitigations.detail: Replace the shared token on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` with short-lived per-pipeline credentials and retain the verified pipeline and initiating-user identity with each release-change event.

mitigations.summary: Record an immutable release-change trail
mitigations.detail: Have `process:deploy-controller` emit structured, append-only audit events containing the prior and new image SHA, verified principal, originating build identifier, timestamp, and outcome.

stride.title: Manual rebuilds may not be attributable to the developer who triggered them
stride.description: A developer can trigger an unreviewed rebuild of main through `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` and later deny having initiated it. That flow crosses from the inferred `boundary:corporate-network` location of `entity:developer` into `boundary:build-environment`, but its `authentication` is unknown. If the unknown authentication does not establish and retain an individual verified principal, neither the rebuild nor the resulting image pushed by `process:build-runner` can be rebuttably tied to the developer who initiated it. The resulting deployment can reach `process:deploy-controller` and then every `process:store-server`; this claim is conditional on the unresolved authentication attribute, not an assertion that no individual authentication or audit record exists.

grounds.text: any developer can log in to the build runner and kick off a rebuild of `main` by hand; that path does not require a merge and is not reviewed

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild:authentication`: a developer must access the internal rebuild path, but the path is available to any developer and crosses into the build environment. Impact is high: `process:build-runner` handles `credentials` and `business-critical-data`, and a rebuild can produce an image that is selected by the deploy controller for the store estate.

mitigations.summary: Require and preserve individual identity for manual rebuilds
mitigations.detail: Use individual, non-shared authentication on `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` and log the verified developer identity, source, requested ref, build ID, timestamp, and result in a protected audit trail.

mitigations.summary: Bind deployments to reviewed build provenance
mitigations.detail: Require the deploy path to retain the initiating identity and immutable build provenance from `process:build-runner` through the release update, so a manual rebuild cannot be indistinguishable from an approved main-branch build.

stride.title: Shared build token may be intercepted on the runner-to-controller crossing
stride.description: `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` crosses from the separate build environment to the corporate network, and its `encryption_in_transit` value is unknown. If that segment lacks effective transport encryption, an attacker able to observe the inter-zone path can intercept the shared build token used by `process:build-runner` to call `process:deploy-controller`, along with the selected image SHA. The disclosed, never-rotated credential enables subsequent access to the deploy-controller release-setting path and therefore supports attacks against releases consumed by the store estate; this threat concerns obtaining the credential, not altering a release.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release:encryption_in_transit`: an attacker must obtain an on-path position across the documented boundary crossing, but the static shared token makes capture immediately reusable. Impact is high because the disclosed credential authorizes the release-setting path of `process:deploy-controller`, whose chosen release is polled by the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt and mutually authenticate the release-setting flow
mitigations.detail: Require TLS 1.2+ with mTLS for `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, validating the deploy controller and build-runner identities across the boundary.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared static build token
mitigations.detail: Issue a distinct, short-lived workload credential per pipeline, scope it only to the required release operation, and rotate the existing shared token.

stride.title: Source code may be readable on the build-runner-to-git-server link
stride.description: `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source` carries the source of the merged commit from `store:git-server` across the build-environment-to-corporate-network boundary, but its `encryption_in_transit` attribute is unknown. If transport protection is absent or terminates before this segment, an on-path attacker can intercept proprietary source code while the build runner fetches it. The acquired code reveals application behavior and dependency choices, enabling more targeted attacks against `process:build-runner`, the build output, and the deployment path.

grounds.text: The build runner picks the merge up, fetches the source, resolves the dependency lockfile and produces a container image.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source:encryption_in_transit`: observing the inter-zone path requires a network foothold, but no transport protection is verified. Impact is medium because the intercepted merged source is business-critical build material and enables reconnaissance against downstream build and deployment components.

mitigations.summary: Protect source retrieval with authenticated TLS
mitigations.detail: Set `encryption_in_transit` for `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source` to TLS or mTLS and validate the git-server identity from the build environment.

mitigations.summary: Restrict visibility of the inter-zone path
mitigations.detail: Segment and monitor the build-environment-to-corporate-network connection so only the runner can reach the git service and unauthorized packet capture or proxying is detected.

stride.title: Store-release images may be readable over the retail WAN
stride.description: `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` crosses from `boundary:store-estate` to `boundary:build-environment` over the WAN, while `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If this pull is not end-to-end encrypted, a party able to observe the retail WAN can intercept container images obtained by each `process:store-server`. Image contents disclose the deployed till software and its implementation details; collecting releases from the fleet enables targeted follow-on attacks against the same software running across approximately 1,200 stores.

grounds.text: The image registry is reachable from the store estate over the WAN.
if it differs from what it is running it pulls that image from the registry and restarts the container.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image:encryption_in_transit`: the attacker needs an on-path position on the documented WAN crossing, but no verified encryption is stated. Impact is medium because the flow distributes business-critical container images to the approximately 1,200-store estate, making one captured image useful for broad implementation reconnaissance.

mitigations.summary: Require encrypted, authenticated image pulls
mitigations.detail: Use TLS 1.2+ for `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, validate the registry certificate, and use mTLS or scoped store credentials for registry access.

mitigations.summary: Minimize sensitive image contents
mitigations.detail: Keep credentials and environment-specific configuration out of container layers, and retrieve runtime secrets only from an appropriate secret-management mechanism.

stride.title: Git-server operational copies may expose source if at-rest encryption is absent
stride.description: `store:git-server` holds developer branches and main, while its `encryption_at_rest` and `data_classification` attributes are unknown. If the unverified at-rest control resolves to unencrypted storage, an attacker or over-privileged operator who obtains a disk, backup, snapshot, or decommissioned volume can read the repository directly without using the normal developer push or build-runner fetch paths. The source disclosure enables targeted attacks on `process:build-runner` and downstream release artifacts. This is conditional on the unknown encryption-at-rest value; it does not assert that the git server is unencrypted.

grounds.text: Developers push their branches to our self-hosted git server
Nobody has documented whether the git server encrypts what it stores

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:store:git-server:encryption_at_rest`: obtaining an operational storage copy requires storage-layer access, but the model verifies no encryption-at-rest control. Impact is medium because `store:git-server` contains the source that feeds the build runner and is tagged business-critical-data, making disclosure useful for targeted follow-on attacks.

mitigations.summary: Establish and enforce encrypted git storage
mitigations.detail: Determine the at-rest posture of `store:git-server`, then require managed-key encryption for its primary volumes, backups, snapshots, replicas, and decommissioned media.

mitigations.summary: Constrain access to repository copies
mitigations.detail: Separate backup and storage-administration principals from repository readers, restrict export permissions, and audit snapshot and backup access.

stride.title: Image-registry operational copies may expose deployed software if at-rest encryption is absent
stride.description: `store:image-registry` retains commit-tagged container images, but its `encryption_at_rest` and `data_classification` attributes are unknown. If storage encryption is absent, someone obtaining an image-registry backup, snapshot, volume, or other storage-layer copy can read the images without authenticating as a store server. The recovered artifacts disclose the till software distributed to `process:store-server` and enable tailored follow-on attacks against the fleet. This is a conditional finding about the unresolved encryption-at-rest attribute, not an assertion that the registry is unencrypted.

grounds.text: It pushes the finished image to our image registry, which is also in the build environment. Images are tagged with the commit sha.
Nobody has documented whether the git server encrypts what it stores, or whether the image registry does.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:store:image-registry:encryption_at_rest`: storage-layer access is required, but encryption is unverified. Impact is medium because `store:image-registry` holds business-critical deployment images that are pulled and executed by store servers across the estate.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt registry data and all operational copies
mitigations.detail: Establish whether `store:image-registry` is encrypted at rest, then enforce managed-key encryption for registry storage, backups, snapshots, replicas, and retired volumes.

mitigations.summary: Limit and monitor artifact export access
mitigations.detail: Use least-privilege registry and storage permissions, separate backup-reader roles from store pull roles, and log or alert on image and snapshot exports.

stride.title: Repeated manual rebuilds can exhaust build-runner capacity and block releases
stride.description: A malicious or compromised `entity:developer` on the corporate network can repeatedly invoke `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, which permits any developer to trigger a rebuild of main without a merge. Each rebuild makes `process:build-runner` fetch source, resolve dependencies, build an image, and push it to `store:image-registry`; repeated requests can consume its finite build CPU, memory, worker slots, dependency-download capacity, or registry throughput faster than a developer spends to submit them. The model does not state admission limits, concurrency bounds, or load shedding for this manually triggered path. Second-order, legitimate merged builds cannot complete while the runner is saturated, delaying releases to `process:store-server` across the estate.

grounds.text: any developer can log in to the build runner and kick off a rebuild of `main` by hand

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the attacker must obtain or abuse developer access from `boundary:corporate-network`, but `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` crosses into the build environment and its authentication is `unknown`. Impact is medium because `process:build-runner` is tagged `business-critical-data` and saturation prevents legitimate builds and consequently delays releases to the approximately 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, while the model does not state that the running tills immediately stop.

mitigations.summary: Bound and meter manual rebuild admission
mitigations.detail: Require reviewed or authorized rebuild requests for `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, apply per-developer concurrency and rate limits, and reject excess rebuild requests before they allocate build-runner resources.

mitigations.summary: Isolate release builds from ad hoc work
mitigations.detail: Use bounded, separate worker capacity or queues for manually requested rebuilds and merged-release builds so flooding the former cannot starve the release path through `process:build-runner`.

stride.title: Flooding the shared deploy controller can prevent estate-wide release polling
stride.description: `process:deploy-controller` is a shared chokepoint: every `process:store-server` polls it over `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release` once per minute to learn the current image sha. If an attacker with a foothold in `boundary:store-estate` floods that cross-boundary flow, or if the flow's `authentication: unknown` resolves to insufficient caller admission, the attacker can exhaust the controller's request-handling capacity with cheap polling requests. The model states no per-store request cap, timeout, backoff, or degradation behavior. Second-order, legitimate polling by the roughly 1,200 store servers fails or queues behind the flood, so the estate cannot learn or retrieve an intended release from `store:image-registry`; recovery or urgent deployment is delayed across all stores.

grounds.text: We run about 1,200 stores.
Every store server asks the deploy controller once a minute what the current release is

severity.justification: Likelihood is low because the attacker needs a foothold in `boundary:store-estate` or the unresolved admission weakness on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`; the flow's authentication and protocol are both `unknown`. Impact is medium because the shared `process:deploy-controller` serves about 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, so a successful flood blocks estate-wide release polling and emergency deployment, but the model does not state that stores cease running their current till containers when polling fails.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate and rate-bound each store poller
mitigations.detail: Establish and enforce a distinct authenticated identity for each `process:store-server` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, with per-store request ceilings and rejection of unauthenticated callers.

mitigations.summary: Prevent polling failures from becoming a controller-wide outage
mitigations.detail: Set short request timeouts, bounded queues, exponential backoff with jitter, and circuit breakers at `process:store-server` and `process:deploy-controller` so overload fails fast instead of accumulating concurrent polls.

stride.title: Unsigned public dependencies can execute with build-runner deployment authority
stride.description: An attacker who can cause `entity:public-package-registry` to return a malicious package named by the lockfile can have that package execute while `process:build-runner` resolves dependencies over `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`. The runner does not verify package signatures, so supplied dependency logic inherits the runner's authority rather than the authority of the public source. This escalates an internet-originating package-supply position into the shared build token's authority on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`: the attacker can produce and publish a malicious image, select it as the current release, and ultimately obtain code execution on the `process:store-server` fleet when servers pull and restart that image.

grounds.text: the lockfile is taken as given — the runner does not verify signatures on what it downloads
The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies` crosses to the internet and has stated-absent package authentication, but exploitation requires an attacker to control or substitute a dependency response. Impact is high: `process:build-runner` can set releases through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, and the resulting image is pulled and restarted by the availability-critical `process:store-server` fleet.

mitigations.summary: Require verified, immutable build dependencies
mitigations.detail: Configure `process:build-runner` to accept only dependencies whose signatures and trusted publisher identities are verified, and resolve from immutable package digests or an internally controlled repository.

mitigations.summary: Isolate dependency execution from deployment authority
mitigations.detail: Resolve and build untrusted dependency content in a sandboxed workload without the shared deployment token; require a separate, narrowly scoped and short-lived identity for `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`.
